- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.5) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.3) or volatile, model often underestimates; adjust upward, especially if recent price is falling.
- Model frequently overshoots after sharp price spikes (e.g., +5+ points in 1–2 days); cap forecast at 1–2% below peak if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of price decline after peak), model often fails to correct; add a 1–3 day lagged mean reversion buffer.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to overreact to short-term sentiment shifts; smooth out 3–5 day moving average of sentiment before adjusting forecast.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “reversal” patterns (e.g., +0.8 → -0.2 → +0.8), model often misreads momentum; use sentiment lag (e.g., 2–3 days ago) to weight forecast adjustment.
- When true outcome is >10% above model, check if sentiment was positive 3–5 days prior — if yes, reduce forecast by 1–2% to avoid overconfidence bias.
- If model forecast is consistently below true outcome by 2–3% over 3–5 days, sentiment is likely neutral or slightly positive — increase forecast by 0.5–1% to align with sentiment drift.
